t: Zionism arose in the late 19th century among the Jews of Central and Eastern Europe, in reaction to new waves of antisemitism and to the Jewish Enlightenment, holding that Jews are a nation with a right to self-determination.

Through settlement, land purchase, the Balfour Declaration of 1917 and the British Mandate, the movement built the institutions of a Jewish quasi-state in Palestine, and David Ben-Gurion declared the State of Israel in 1948.

Its advocates see a national liberation movement returning an indigenous people to its ancestral homeland; Palestinians and other opponents see a colonial or settler-colonial movement, pointing to the expulsion and flight of Palestinians in 1948, which Palestinians call the Nakba.
dyk: The word “Zionism” was first used by the Austrian writer Nathan Birnbaum in an article of 1890. Theodor Herzl, unaware of this, popularized the word himself, and did not call himself a Zionist until months after publishing Der Judenstaat in 1896.
ev: The Bilu group, one of the Lovers of Zion, establishes its first settlement in Palestine, the first of several aliyahs
Theodor Herzl publishes Der Judenstaat (“The Jewish State”), calling for the creation of a Jewish state
The First Zionist Congress at Basel founds the Zionist Organization and adopts the Basel Program
In the Balfour Declaration Britain supports “the establishment in Palestine of a national home for the Jewish people”
The British Mandate for Palestine, based on the Balfour Declaration, makes the Jewish Agency a partner of the mandatory government
During the Arab Revolt of 1936–1939, the Peel Commission proposes partition and a transfer of Palestinian Arabs
The United Nations General Assembly votes to partition Palestine into separate Jewish and Arab states
Ben-Gurion declares the State of Israel; in the war of 1948–1949 an estimated 710,000 Palestinians are driven out

f.where: Founded among the Jews of Central and Eastern Europe, above all the Russian Empire’s Pale of Settlement, Poland and Austria; its settlement in Palestine, under Ottoman and then British rule, and from 1948 the State of Israel; support and lobbying in Britain, the United States and the Jewish diaspora.
f.period: Forerunners and the Lovers of Zion (1860s–1890s; first settlement 1882); the First Zionist Congress and the Basel Program (1897); the Second Aliyah (from 1904); the Balfour Declaration (1917) and the British Mandate (1922–1948); the Biltmore Program (1942); the 1948 war and the State of Israel; since then Israel’s dominant ideology.
f.figures: Theodor Herzl, author of Der Judenstaat and convener of the First Zionist Congress; Leon Pinsker, author of Auto-Emancipation; Ahad Ha’am, founder of cultural Zionism; Chaim Weizmann, head of the World Zionist Organization; David Ben-Gurion, Labor Zionist leader who declared the State of Israel; Ze’ev Jabotinsky, founder of Revisionist Zionism; Abraham Isaac Kook, religious Zionist thinker.
f.outcome: The State of Israel, declared on 14 May 1948, which by the end of the war controlled over 78% of former Mandatory Palestine; the 1948 Palestinian expulsion and flight, in which an estimated 710,000 Palestinians were driven out; the immigration of Jews from Europe, the Soviet Union and the Arab world; a lasting conflict with the Palestinians and a sharp debate over the movement’s nature.
